Slices

Install features, not components. One command writes the UI, the service behind it and the resources it needs — into your repo, and it stays yours.

By Séverin Marcombes · slices.sh

Every component registry stops at the same place. It hands you a beautiful table and wishes you luck. But a table is never just a table — it is a view onto a collection, and a collection means auth, an audit trail, a database, and a route that filters what each user is allowed to see. The registry gives you one of those six things and leaves you the other five.

Slices is one layer past that. It is a shadcn-compatible registry of fullstack features: the UI, the behaviour underneath it, the hooks, the client and server SDKs, the access rules, the API route, and the resources the whole thing needs to actually run.

A table is never just a table.

What one command actually writes

This is the whole argument, and it is easier to show than to describe. One add, and what lands in the repository: 

$ npx shadcn add https://slices.sh/r/collection-table

✓ components/molecules/collection-table/     the skin
✓ components/skinnable/collection-table/     the pattern, platform-neutral
✓ components/headless/collection/            behaviour, no opinion on looks
✓ hooks/collection/                          one file per hook
✓ services/collection/                       client SDK, server SDK, types
✓ services/auth/rules.ts                     yours, seeded once
✓ app/api/collections/[collection]/route.ts  a real REST route

One command wrote six directories, including your API route. I do not know of another registry in this category that can make that claim.

The code is yours, and there is no runtime

Installation is copy-in, exactly as shadcn does it. There is no package to depend on, no version to bump, no dispatcher sitting where your routes should be. After installing, nothing in the resulting code says a registry was ever involved: no shared implementation folder, no framework fingerprints, no vendor name in a path.

That constraint is not aesthetic. Code you cannot read and edit is code you cannot own, and a feature you do not own is a dependency you will eventually fight.

Swap the backend, keep the contract

Underneath each feature is a contract, and a contract can have several implementations that all pass the same conformance suite. The UI never learns which one you picked, so changing your mind is one more add rather than a rewrite.

  • → collection — memory, SQLite, MongoDB, Supabase.
  • → auth — devlogin, Better Auth, Clerk, BotParty.
  • → ai-chat — echo, Vercel AI SDK. file-storage — memory, S3.
  • → audit, geocoder and realtime have one implementation each — enough to prove the seam is real, not enough to prove a swap.

When a contract has exactly one implementation it is served verbatim and the consumer never learns there was a choice. With several, it becomes a placeholder that names them. That is the entire resolution rule.

The resources come too

This is what makes “end-to-end” literal rather than aspirational. A feature declares the resources it needs, and the accessor does not fail with a stack trace — it fails with the command that fixes it: 

The "mongo" resource is not configured.
Missing environment variables: MONGODB_URI
Provision it in one command:
  npx extraorbital provision mongo

ExtraOrbital reads the project, creates the database, bucket, queue or model key on a free tier, and writes the variables back into the environment. No console, no card, nobody in the loop — which is also precisely what makes the whole path runnable by an agent.

slices add → extraorbital provision → the feature runs.

One pattern, three libraries

There are 27 patterns across 6 families, each shipped for coss, shadcn-radix and shadcn-baseui — 90 molecules in total. Under every one of them sits a skinnable that names no platform at all, so a fourth skin, or a React Native one, is a map of class names rather than a rewrite.

One pattern carries variants: document-viewer is a single contract, a single skinnable and a single documentation page, installed four ways — PDF, DOCX, XLSX, PPTX — so a project ships only the parsers it actually uses.

Why build it this shape

The objection is never “I cannot find a table component”. It is “I will just ask the model to write it”. That answer has a bill, and the tokens are the cheapest line on it.

You pay in tokens, burning a million of them on a sign-in screen, then again next sprint, then again on the next project. You pay in risk, because generated auth is code nobody has read twice, and access rules are exactly where rows leak — a model hands you a confident, plausible, subtly wrong one that looks identical to a correct one in the diff. And you pay in attention: every hour re-checking generated plumbing is an hour not spent on the part only you can build.

A slice has already been read. Sign-in, invitations, collections and audit trails are generic — the same in your product and in mine — and there is no reason for either of us to invent them privately. Every implementation passes the same conformance suite before it ships, a bug is fixed in one place, and you add again instead of prompting again.

Which is the same argument I would make about agents generally. An agent is not just a model and a harness; it needs muscle memory, and muscle memory should be executable software rather than prose — something that runs deterministically, is evaluated against the real world, and improves in one place for everyone. Slices is that idea aimed at the audience best equipped to judge it: developers, who will notice immediately if the code is not good.
